summary: Identifies common roles of SIP back-to-back user agents, such as IP PBXs, session border controllers and application servers, which go beyond proxies. It is a taxonomy.

plainLanguage.summary: A SIP back-to-back user agent can change signaling, media descriptions, or the media itself. This memo names common roles according to which parts of a session the device handles.

questions: what is the difference between a sip proxy and a b2bua
what is a session border controller
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for the different roles performed by SIP back-to-back user agents.

tldr.problem: SIP devices in the signaling path often do more than a proxy, but the term B2BUA covers a wide range of behaviors.
tldr.mechanism: The memo divides B2BUA behavior into signaling-only roles and roles that also process or relay media.
tldr.outcome: It gives names for common roles so other documents can refer to them consistently. It is an Informational taxonomy, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 7092 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo defines role terminology rather than protocol behavior.

sections.title: What a B2BUA Means
sections.content:
A Back-to-Back User Agent (B2BUA) is the logical combination of a User Agent Server and a User Agent Client. The memo classifies the role a system performs, not the product category or physical box. One system can change roles during a session.

The memo distinguishes a B2BUA from a typical centralized conference server, where multiple clients establish separate sessions to one server. An inline conference-bridge transcoder can be a B2BUA, while the third-party call-control transcoder described in RFC 5369 is not.
sections.plainLanguage: A B2BUA acts as both a server-side and client-side SIP user agent. The role describes what it does in a session, not the name of the device.

sections.title: Signaling-Only Roles
sections.content:
A signaling-plane B2BUA handles SIP messages but does not handle the media itself. A Proxy-B2BUA appears like a proxy but keeps enough dialog state to send its own in-dialog messages, such as a BYE. It does not modify most received headers or inspect MIME bodies.

A Signaling-only B2BUA can modify SIP headers or selected bodies beyond proxy behavior. An SDP-modifying signaling-only B2BUA also changes SDP, but does not join the media path. An example is changing codec choices in the session description.
sections.plainLanguage: Some B2BUAs change only SIP signaling, while others also edit the session description. These roles do not carry the media stream themselves.

sections.title: Roles That Also Handle Media
sections.content:
A signaling-and-media B2BUA acts on SIP and media-plane information. A Media Relay terminates media at the IP and transport layers and copies the payload between its sides without changing its contents. It may also police packets or convert between IPv4 and IPv6.

A Media Aware B2BUA can inspect or change transport payloads, such as RTP or RTCP, but does not process them at the codec layer. A Media Termination B2BUA works with the media payload, for example by converting codecs or acting on MSRP messages. The logical B2BUA may be split across separate signaling and media systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A media relay forwards media payloads, a media-aware device can inspect or alter them, and a media-termination device works with the media content itself.

sections.title: How Device Categories Map to Roles
sections.content:
SIP PBXs and softswitches are market categories rather than terms defined by a standard. Depending on their architecture or local policy, they can perform any of the roles in the taxonomy. Application servers also vary: some handle signaling only, while others terminate media.

Session Border Controllers likewise can perform different roles; the memo says many commonly operate as media relays or media-aware B2BUAs. Transcoders perform media termination. Conference servers generally are not B2BUAs, with an exception when a conference function triggers multiple INVITEs as a user agent client.
sections.plainLanguage: A product label does not determine a B2BUA role. A PBX, application server, or session border controller may perform different roles depending on its configuration and function.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security risks vary by B2BUA role. Adding systems to the communication path creates additional attack points, can reduce end-to-end encryption, affects privacy, and complicates trust relationships.

The memo specifically notes that processing SDP and media can impede end-to-end SRTP, while the ability to alter SIP headers or bodies affects identity and message integrity. Management and configuration mechanisms also need strong protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each intermediary adds a system that must be trusted and secured. A B2BUA that changes signaling or media can also limit end-to-end protections.
